definition: Miniaturized devices that combine mechanical structures (beams, membranes, gears) with electrical circuitry, with feature sizes from about 1 to 100 micrometres. Typical examples are accelerometers, gyroscopes, pressure sensors and micromirrors.

Electromechanical devices with at least one critical dimension below about 100 nm. At this scale surface effects, intermolecular forces and quantum effects become significant, enabling ultra-sensitive mass, force and charge sensing.
related: MEMS; Size effect; Casimir force; Nanoresonator

definition: The dependence of a material's or structure's mechanical response (stiffness, strength, frequency) on its absolute size. Classical continuum mechanics has no intrinsic length scale and cannot capture it, which motivates non-classical theories.
related: Length-scale parameter; Strain gradient theory; Nonlocal elasticity

definition: A material constant with the dimension of length introduced in non-classical continuum theories to represent micro-structural effects. It is usually identified from experiments or atomistic simulations.
related: Size effect; Modified couple stress theory; Strain gradient theory

definition: The ratio of surface area to volume of a body, which grows as 1/size. At the nanoscale a large fraction of atoms sit at the surface, so surface energy and surface stress dominate the response.

Rules describing how physical quantities change with size. Inertia (∝ L³) shrinks faster than surface forces (∝ L²) and electrostatic forces, so at small scales friction, adhesion and electrostatics dominate gravity and inertia.
related: Plenty of Room at the Bottom; Stiction

term: Plenty of Room at the Bottom
definition: Title of Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture at Caltech that envisioned writing encyclopaedias on a pin head, building tiny machines and manipulating individual atoms — widely regarded as the conceptual birth of nanotechnology.
A device that converts energy from one domain to another — e.g. mechanical to electrical (sensor) or electrical to mechanical (actuator). Most MEMS are electromechanical transducers.

Driving a movable electrode by the Coulomb attraction between oppositely charged conductors. The force grows with V² and decreases with the gap, making it simple and low-power but intrinsically nonlinear.

The loss of static equilibrium of an electrostatically actuated structure when the voltage exceeds a critical value: the elastic restoring force can no longer balance the electrostatic force and the electrode suddenly collapses onto the substrate. For a parallel-plate model it occurs at one third of the initial gap.
related: Pull-in voltage; Electrostatic actuation; Dynamic pull-in

definition: The critical voltage at which pull-in instability occurs. It sets the operating range of switches, tweezers and actuators and is strongly affected by size effects and intermolecular forces.

Pull-in triggered by a suddenly applied (step) or time-varying voltage. Because of inertia it occurs at a lower voltage than static pull-in — about 92% of the static value for an undamped parallel-plate model.
The voltage below which a collapsed electrode is released again. It is lower than the pull-in voltage, producing hysteresis, and may be zero if adhesion (stiction) holds the electrode down.

An attractive force between closely spaced uncharged conductors caused by quantum vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field. It dominates for gaps of roughly 20 nm to a few micrometres and can cause pull-in without any applied voltage.
related: van der Waals force; Pull-in instability; Quantum MEMS

definition: A short-range attraction between atoms and molecules due to induced dipoles. In NEMS it is significant for gaps below about 20 nm and lowers the pull-in voltage.
The material-dependent constant that scales the van der Waals interaction between two bodies, typically 10⁻²⁰ – 10⁻¹⁹ J.
The part of the electric field that bulges out at the edges of electrodes. It increases the effective electrostatic force, especially for narrow beams, and must be corrected in accurate models.
Unintended permanent adhesion of microstructures to the substrate caused by capillary, van der Waals, electrostatic or hydrogen-bonding forces — a major failure mode in MEMS.
Damping caused by the viscous flow of gas squeezed out of a narrow gap by a moving plate. It often dominates energy loss in MEMS operating at atmospheric pressure.
A measure of how lightly damped a resonator is: the ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle (×2π). High-Q NEMS resonators can detect masses down to single molecules.
The natural frequency at which a structure vibrates with maximum amplitude. Small, stiff and light structures resonate at MHz–GHz frequencies.
Detecting added mass from the shift it causes in the resonant frequency of a resonator. NEMS sensitivity reaches the zeptogram (10⁻²¹ g) range.
A nonlinear oscillator with a cubic stiffness term. It describes hardening or softening resonance, jump phenomena and bistability in micro/nano beams.
formula: mẍ + cẋ + kx + k₃x³ = F cos ωt

definition: Vibration in which the restoring force, damping or excitation depends nonlinearly on the motion — producing amplitude-dependent frequency, multiple solutions and chaos.
A qualitative change in a system's equilibria or periodic solutions as a parameter varies. Pull-in is a saddle-node bifurcation of the static equilibrium.
The existence of two stable equilibria separated by an unstable one. Bistable beams are used in switches, memories and broadband energy harvesters.
Resonance excited by periodic modulation of a system parameter (e.g. stiffness) rather than a direct force, typically at twice the natural frequency.
Theories of elasticity in which stress at a point depends only on strain at that point and no intrinsic length exists. They fail to predict size-dependent behavior of micro/nano structures.
Extensions of classical elasticity that include one or more length-scale parameters to capture size effects — e.g. nonlocal, strain-gradient, couple-stress and surface-elasticity theories.
related: Nonlocal elasticity; Strain gradient theory; Modified couple stress theory

definition: A theory in which the stress at a point depends on strains at all points of the body, weighted by a kernel. In differential form it introduces the nonlocal parameter (e₀a)².
A well-posed integral nonlocal formulation in which the strain is obtained as a convolution of the stress field, avoiding paradoxes of Eringen's differential model for bounded structures.
A theory in which the strain energy depends on strain and its spatial gradients, introducing higher-order stresses and length-scale parameters. It typically predicts stiffer behavior at small sizes.
related: Modified couple stress theory; Length-scale parameter

definition: A simplified couple-stress theory (Yang et al., 2002) with a single material length-scale parameter, where strain energy depends on strain and the symmetric curvature tensor.
related: Strain gradient theory; Consistent couple stress theory

definition: A couple-stress formulation in which the couple-stress tensor is skew-symmetric, proposed to resolve indeterminacy in earlier couple-stress models.

A model that treats the surface of a solid as a membrane of zero thickness with its own elastic constants and residual stress, perfectly bonded to the bulk. It captures surface effects in nanostructures.
Changes in mechanical behavior due to surface energy, surface stress and surface elasticity, which become important when the surface-to-volume ratio is large.
Calculus with derivatives and integrals of non-integer order (e.g. Caputo, Riemann–Liouville). Used to model memory and long-range interactions in viscoelastic and nonlocal materials.
The classical slender-beam model in which plane sections remain plane and perpendicular to the neutral axis; shear deformation and rotary inertia are neglected.
A beam theory that includes shear deformation and rotary inertia, needed for short or thick beams and higher modes.
A beam fixed at one end and free at the other — the most common MEMS/NEMS building block in sensors, AFM probes and tweezers.
A beam fixed at both ends. It is stiffer than a cantilever and develops axial (stretching) nonlinearity at large deflection.
Gripping devices made of two (or more) nano-arms — such as carbon nanotubes or nanowires — that close electrostatically to pick and place nano-objects. Their range is limited by pull-in.
A micro-scale gripping device, often based on compliant mechanisms and driven by electrostatic, electrothermal or piezoelectric actuators.
A NEMS switch whose movable electrode closes a circuit when pulled in. Offers near-zero leakage and abrupt switching for low-power logic and memory.
A nanoscale vibrating structure (beam, membrane, tube) used for mass, force or charge sensing, filtering and timing.
A nano-positioning device that scans a probe or mirror by bending and/or torsion, used in scanning probe microscopy and optical scanning.
A stage that moves an object with nanometre resolution, typically using piezoelectric or electrostatic actuation and flexure guides.
An electrostatic actuator made of interdigitated finger electrodes. The force is nearly independent of displacement, giving a larger stable stroke than parallel plates.
A MEMS inertial sensor that measures acceleration from the displacement of a suspended proof mass, usually read out capacitively.
A vibratory angular-rate sensor that detects rotation through the Coriolis force acting on a driven proof mass.
A sensor that detects biological species (proteins, DNA, cells) by converting a binding event into a measurable signal — in NEMS, usually a frequency shift or static deflection.
A scanning probe microscope that images surfaces by sensing the deflection of a sharp tip on a micro-cantilever. It is also a fundamental tool for nanomanipulation.
A device that converts ambient energy (vibration, heat, light) into electricity for self-powered sensors, using piezoelectric, electrostatic, electromagnetic or triboelectric transduction.
A mechanism that transmits motion and force through elastic deformation of flexible members instead of joints — ideal for MEMS because it avoids friction, wear and assembly.
A thin, flexible section that acts as a rotational joint in a compliant mechanism, offering backlash-free, high-resolution motion.
A cylindrical nanostructure of rolled graphene sheets with extraordinary stiffness (≈1 TPa), strength and conductivity — used in nanotweezers, resonators and switches.
A single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal lattice. Extremely stiff, strong and light, it is ideal for ultra-sensitive membrane resonators and pressure sensors.
Crystalline materials only one or a few atomic layers thick — graphene, MoS₂, h-BN, MXenes — with unique mechanical, electrical and optical properties.
A family of 2D transition-metal carbides and nitrides (e.g. Ti₃C₂Tₓ) with metallic conductivity and hydrophilic surfaces, promising for sensors and energy devices.
A one-dimensional nanostructure with diameter of a few to hundreds of nanometres, made of metals or semiconductors.
The generation of electric charge in certain crystals (PZT, AlN, ZnO) under mechanical stress, and the converse deformation under an electric field. Used in sensors, actuators and harvesters.
Charge transfer between two different materials upon contact and separation — the basis of triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs).
An engineered material with a negative Poisson's ratio: it becomes thicker when stretched. Its unusual deformation can tune stiffness and stability of actuators.
An architected material whose properties come from its structure rather than its composition, enabling stiffness, wave or thermal behavior not found in nature.
Material behavior combining elastic (spring-like) and viscous (dashpot-like) response, leading to creep, relaxation and damping.
The set of processes — lithography, deposition, etching, bonding — used to make micro-devices, mostly derived from integrated-circuit technology.
Patterning a light-sensitive resist with UV light through a mask; the pattern is then transferred into the material by etching or deposition.
Building structures from thin films deposited on a substrate and released by removing a sacrificial layer.
Making structures by etching deep into the substrate itself, e.g. anisotropic KOH etching or deep reactive-ion etching.
A plasma etching process (e.g. the Bosch process) that creates deep, high-aspect-ratio vertical trenches in silicon.
A numerical method that approximates derivatives as weighted sums of function values at grid points. Highly accurate with few points — widely used for nonlinear beam and plate problems.
A weighted-residual method that projects the governing equation onto a set of trial functions (e.g. mode shapes), reducing a PDE to ordinary differential equations.
A numerical technique that divides a domain into elements and solves for approximate fields — the standard tool for multiphysics MEMS design (COMSOL, ANSYS, ABAQUS).
A semi-analytical series method for nonlinear differential equations, used to obtain closed-form approximate solutions for pull-in of nano-beams.
A semi-analytical technique that deforms a simple problem continuously into the nonlinear one, producing series solutions.
An approximate analytical method for nonlinear oscillators based on the Hamiltonian, giving amplitude–frequency relations in closed form.
A frequency-domain method that approximates steady-state periodic responses of nonlinear systems by truncated Fourier series.
A mesoscopic fluid-simulation method based on particle distribution functions on a lattice, suited to micro-flows and complex boundaries.
A low-dimensional model that captures the essential dynamics of a large system (e.g. via POD or Galerkin projection) for fast simulation and control.
Simultaneous modeling of interacting physical fields — mechanical, electrical, thermal, fluidic, magnetic — typical of MEMS/NEMS.
A neural network trained to satisfy the governing differential equations and boundary conditions by including their residuals in the loss function, needing little or no labelled data.
A fast approximation (neural network, Gaussian process, polynomial) of an expensive simulation, used for design optimization and uncertainty quantification.
A Bayesian non-parametric regression method that returns both a prediction and its uncertainty.
The integration of machine learning with physical laws and numerical methods to build accurate, data-efficient and interpretable models of engineering systems.
A virtual replica of a physical system that is continuously updated with sensor data to monitor, predict and optimize its behavior in real time.
A learning paradigm in which an agent learns a control policy by interacting with an environment and maximizing cumulative reward (e.g. PPO, DDPG).
Control based on fuzzy logic rules (IF–THEN) with linguistic variables, effective for nonlinear systems that are hard to model exactly.
Controller design that guarantees stability and performance despite model uncertainty and disturbances (e.g. H∞, sliding mode, QFT).
Quantitative Feedback Theory — a frequency-domain robust control method that shapes the loop on the Nichols chart to meet specifications over a set of uncertain plants.
Systematic characterization of how uncertainties in inputs (e.g. length-scale parameters) propagate to model predictions.
Mechanical resonators operated in or near the quantum regime, where phonons, vacuum fluctuations and opto-mechanical coupling become observable and useful.
A transducer that converts a physical quantity (acceleration, pressure, mass, temperature) into a measurable — usually electrical — signal.
A transducer that converts an input signal (usually electrical) into mechanical motion or force — e.g. electrostatic, piezoelectric, electrothermal or magnetic actuators.
Science and engineering of matter at roughly 1–100 nm, where size-dependent properties emerge; the field Feynman anticipated in 1959.
related: Plenty of Room at the Bottom; NEMS

definition: Reading the displacement of a structure from the change in capacitance between it and a fixed electrode — the most common MEMS readout.
The simplest electrostatic actuator: a movable plate on a spring facing a fixed electrode. Its stable travel is limited to one third of the initial gap by pull-in.
Dependence of a system's state on its history — e.g. the gap between pull-in and pull-out voltages, or between up- and down-sweep frequency responses of a Duffing resonator.
A model that represents flexible members of a compliant mechanism by rigid links connected with torsional springs at characteristic pivots, enabling fast kinematic and force analysis.
The excess energy per unit area at a surface compared with the bulk; together with surface stress it governs size-dependent behavior of nanostructures.
Coating a sensor surface with receptor molecules (antibodies, aptamers) so that it binds only the target analyte.
